passages.text: Simon said, ‘My argument with you from the beginning was to expose you from the scriptures as lying when you say one must not speak of many gods. That is why I showed many written utterances: the divine scriptures themselves speak of many gods.’ Peter said, ‘The very scriptures that speak of many gods themselves also brought this before us, saying, “The names of other gods shall not rise upon your lips.” So I did not speak against what is written, Simon.’ Simon said, ‘Listen to a reply to that too, Peter. You seem to me to sin in speaking against them, since scripture says, “You shall not speak evil, and you shall not speak badly of a ruler of your people.”’ Peter said, ‘I do not sin, Simon, in foretelling their destruction in agreement with the scriptures. For it is written, “Gods who did not make heaven and earth, let them perish.” This does not mean, as you interpreted it, that some did make them and will not perish. For the maker is shown to be one by what is written from the beginning: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” It did not say “the gods.” Somewhere else it says, “The firmament announces the work of his hands.” And in another place it is written, “The heavens themselves will perish, but you will remain forever.”’

lexical_decisions.chosen: themselves also brought this before us, saying
lexical_decisions.rationale: The printed form is treated as a form of παράγω, bringing forward or passing by. The main text preserves its presentation sense, with this pointing to the following quotation. A material intransitive alternative is passed before us, saying. The quoted prohibition functions as instruction, but that function is not substituted for the movement or presentation verb; no Greek correction is supplied.
The term denotes the established heavenly expanse in the quoted cosmological language. It is not modernized into a scientifically specified atmosphere or an otherwise unexpressed material dome.

passages.text: Simon said, ‘To show that there are many gods, I presented clear utterances from the scriptures. You have brought as many, or even more, utterances from those same scriptures to show that there is one God, the God of the Jews. In answer to my saying that one must not speak evil of gods, you added, to show that there is one maker, that those who did not make must perish. In answer to my saying that one must speak of gods, since the scriptures also speak of them, you showed that one must not utter their names, because the same scripture says not to utter the names of other gods. Since, then, the scriptures themselves say that there are many gods and at other times that there is only one, and sometimes say not to speak evil of them and at other times to speak evil of them, what must we conclude from this except that the scriptures themselves mislead us?’

lexical_decisions.rationale: The question is about the inference required by the stated premises, retaining the necessity expressed by δεῖ rather than substituting mere ability.
The term means leading astray or deceiving, not merely presenting a neutral diversity of views. Its accusation is retained as Simon's argument.

passages.text: Simon said, ‘Since I see you speaking more frequently on behalf of the God who fashioned you, learn from me how you are impious even toward him. The makers appear to be two, as scripture says, “And God said, Let us make a human in our image and according to likeness.” “Let us make” indicates two or more, but certainly not one.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Ποιήσωμεν ἄνθρωπον κατ’ εἰκόνα ἡμετέραν καὶ καθ’ ὁμοίωσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Let us make a human in our image and according to likeness
lexical_decisions.rationale: The plural deliberative form and our are central to Simon's inference and retained. The second phrase does not repeat an expressed possessive, so the English does not add a second our.

passages.text: Peter answered, ‘Whether scriptures or prophets speak of gods, they speak to test their hearers. For it is written: “If a prophet arises among you, giving you signs and wonders, and that sign and wonder comes to pass, but he says to you, ‘Let us go and worship other gods whom your fathers did not know,’ you shall not listen to that prophet. Your hands shall be the first to stone him, for he tempted you to turn away from the Lord your God. If you say in your heart, ‘How did he perform that sign or wonder?’ you shall surely know that the tempter was testing you to see whether you fear the Lord your God.” It was said that the tempter was testing, but it appears differently after the removal to Babylon. For God, who knows everything (as can be shown from many passages), would not test in order to learn for himself, since he knows everything beforehand. If you wish, we will discuss this, and I will show that God has foreknowledge. The claim that he is ignorant has been shown to be false and itself written as a test. Thus, Simon, we cannot be made to stumble either by scriptures or by anyone else; neither are we deceived into accepting many gods, nor do we agree with any statement spoken against God.’

lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle plus finite verb repeats the knowing root for emphasis. The main rendering expresses that assurance without adding a new source of knowledge.
The repeated testing root is retained, with tempter distinguishing the agent from God in Peter's stated argument. The noun is not silently replaced by a personal name.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἑτέρως δὲ μετὰ τὴν εἰς Βαβυλῶνα μετοικεσίαν φαίνεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: but it appears differently after the removal to Babylon
lexical_decisions.rationale: The clause asserts a difference in presentation after the Babylonian displacement. It does not specify a scribe, manuscript, or exact replacement wording, so none is supplied.

passages.text: ‘For we ourselves know from the scriptures that angels have been called gods: I mean the one who spoke at the bush and wrestled with Jacob, as well as the one born as Emmanuel and the one called Mighty God. Moreover, Moses became a god to Pharaoh, though in reality he was a human. So too the idols of the nations. But for us there is one God, one: the one who made created things and ordered everything, whose son the Messiah is. In obedience to him, we recognize the false things in the scriptures. Moreover, supplied by the fathers with the true things of the scriptures, we know only one who made the heavens and the earth, the God of the Jews and of all who choose to worship him. The fathers, declaring this to be true by reasoning that loves God, handed him down to us, so that we might know that anything said against God is false. But I will say something even beyond this: if things are not as I have said, may it be my lot, and that of those who love the truth, to run the risk for speaking well of the God who made us.’

lexical_decisions.rationale: The following examples remain within Peter's statement about appellations. Their inclusion is retained without imposing or repairing the author's classification to fit a later theological system.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὗ καὶ ὁ χριστὸς υἱός, ᾧ πειθόμενοι
lexical_decisions.chosen: whose son the Messiah is. In obedience to him
lexical_decisions.rationale: Christos functions independently as a title, so Messiah follows the supplied policy. The relative him is grammatically compatible with the Messiah or God; the main text leaves the pronoun unexpanded rather than resolving that attachment silently.

lexical_decisions.chosen: declaring this to be true by reasoning that loves God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adjective can mean God-loving or beloved by God. The argument's insistence on reverent thinking supports the active sense; reasoning dear to God is a material alternative. The truth qualification is retained without adding a new creed.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: περὶ εὐφημίας τοῦ πεποιηκότος ἡμᾶς θεοῦ κινδυνεύειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: to run the risk for speaking well of the God who made us
lexical_decisions.rationale: The willingness to risk being wrong is explicitly tied to reverent speech about the creator. The translation does not turn it into a denial that any risk exists.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ ἐπὶ τῆς βάτου λαλήσας καὶ τῷ Ἰακὼβ παλαίσας
lexical_decisions.chosen: the one who spoke at the bush and wrestled with Jacob
lexical_decisions.rationale: The first two participles share the single article ὁ, which motivates a shared-subject rendering. This differs from the repeated articles before the subsequent Emmanuel and Mighty God designations. The English preserves that grammatical pattern without independently assigning the subject a later theological identity.
